title: Using a wheelchair for longer distances with arthritis: getting one, staying active and getting out (UK guide)
meta_title: Wheelchair for Longer Distances With Arthritis (UK)

direct_answer: Many people with arthritis can walk around the house but find longer distances, such as shopping, hospital corridors or days out, too painful or tiring. Using a wheelchair just for those trips is not giving up: it can get you out more and save your energy for the things you enjoy. Ask your GP, physiotherapist or occupational therapist about a referral to your local NHS wheelchair service if you need one long term, hire one from the British Red Cross for short-term needs, and get advice before buying. Keep walking short distances every day and keep up strength exercises so your legs stay strong. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.

content:
If arthritis means you can manage around the house but longer distances leave you in pain, exhausted or unsteady, a wheelchair used only for those trips can give you your life back. This guide covers when it helps, how to get one through the NHS or hire one, what to think about before buying, and how to keep your legs strong at the same time.

It is for people with arthritis who walk less far than they used to, and for the family or friends who push. If you are still deciding between aids, start with walking aids for arthritis. If you only need a chair for a few weeks, for example after an operation or for a holiday, see short-term equipment loans.

When a wheelchair for distance makes sense

Signs it may help include: you plan trips around where you can sit down, you avoid shops, hospitals or family days out because of the walking, you pay for a long walk with days of pain, or you have had falls or near-falls when tired. A part-time wheelchair lets you get there and still have energy to enjoy it. Many people use one for distance and keep walking with a stick or frame at home.

A wheelchair does not mean your arthritis has “won”. Pacing your energy is a core part of managing arthritis pain, and a chair is one way of doing that.

Getting a wheelchair through the NHS

  • Ask your GP, physiotherapist or occupational therapist to refer you to your local NHS wheelchair service. Some services also accept self-referral.
  • Services usually provide chairs for people with a long-term need. Rules vary by area, so ask what your local service covers.
  • At the assessment, describe your worst days, how far you can walk before you need to stop, any falls, and where you want to go, including getting the chair in and out of a car.
  • Ask whether a personal wheelchair budget is available, which may let you put money towards a different chair.

Hiring or borrowing for short-term needs

The British Red Cross hires out wheelchairs in many areas for short-term use. Some shopping centres and town centres run Shopmobility schemes where you can borrow a wheelchair or scooter for the day, and many hospitals, museums and attractions have chairs you can borrow if you ask in advance.

Buying a wheelchair: questions to ask first

  • Who will push it? If a partner with their own joint problems will push, a lighter chair with good handles and attendant brakes matters.
  • Self-propelling or transit? Self-propelling chairs have large back wheels you push with your hands, which can be hard on arthritic wrists, hands and shoulders. Transit chairs are lighter and need someone to push.
  • Getting it in the car: check the folded size and weight, and try lifting it yourself.
  • Comfort: seat height and width, a pressure-relieving cushion if you sit for long, and footplates that swing away so you can stand up safely.
  • VAT relief: if you have a long-term condition such as arthritis, you may not have to pay VAT on a wheelchair bought for your own use. Ask the seller.

Try before you buy where possible, and ask an occupational therapist or physiotherapist for advice. Living Made Easy, run by the Disabled Living Foundation, has impartial information on types of chair.

Keep walking and keep your legs strong

Using a chair for distance works best alongside daily movement. Keep walking short distances at home and outdoors on good days, and keep up simple strength exercises, such as standing up from a chair several times with control. NICE recommends exercise as a core treatment for osteoarthritis. A physiotherapist can give you a plan that suits your joints. See staying steady at home with knee osteoarthritis for ideas.

Safety in and out of the chair

  • Always put both brakes on before getting in or out, and swing the footplates out of the way before you stand.
  • Stand up the way you would from any chair: shuffle forward, feet back, push up from the armrests. Never stand on the footplates.
  • Pushers: go down kerbs backwards, keep your back straight and ask for help on steep slopes.
  • Check tyres and brakes regularly.

Getting out and about

  • A Blue Badge may let you park closer to where you are going.
  • For trains, book Passenger Assist in advance for help boarding and ramps.
  • If you have a higher rate of the mobility part of PIP or similar benefits, the Motability Scheme may help with a wheelchair or a car.
  • If you need more independence outdoors, compare with a mobility scooter.

When to see your GP

Book a GP or physiotherapy appointment if your walking distance is getting shorter over weeks or months, you are having falls, or pain stops you sleeping. Your GP can review your pain relief, refer you for physiotherapy or a falls assessment, and refer you to the wheelchair service.

Get urgent help from NHS 111 or your GP the same day if a joint becomes hot, red and swollen, or you suddenly cannot put weight on a leg. Call 999 if you have a fall and cannot get up, are badly hurt, or have chest pain or sudden weakness.

For carers and family

Suggest the chair as a way to do more, not less. Let the person decide when to use it. If pushing hurts your own back or joints, say so: a lighter chair, a power pack or a carer’s assessment from the council may help.

Common questions

Will using a wheelchair make my legs weaker?

Not if you keep walking and exercising for the rest of the day. Many people find they walk more at home because they are not worn out from long trips.

Can I get a wheelchair on the NHS if I can still walk?

Possibly. Ask to be referred and explain how far you can walk and what you are missing out on. Each service sets its own criteria.

Can I hire a wheelchair for a holiday?

Yes. The British Red Cross and many private suppliers hire chairs for short periods.
